messages.author: 661599c031af2f3f
messages.subject: Equality constraints on standardized estimates
parts:
Dear Yves, others,
I was wondering whether it would be possible to equality constrain standardized coefficients? I appreciate this would have non trivial consequences for the optimisation algorithm but there are situations where it would be rather useful (e.g. when comparing the strength of some predictor on two outcomes on different scales). Scaling the outcome variables would represent only an approximate solution..
Best,
Rogier

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Equality constraints on standardized estimates
parts: I was wondering whether it would be possible to equality constrain standardized coefficients?

You could define standardized estimates as new parameters in your model syntax, then try constraining those to equality.  You standardize a regression slope by multiplying the raw slope by the ratio of SD(predictor) / SD(outcome), regardless of the number of predictors.  If they are observed variables, it is easy to check your descriptive stats and directly enter a numerical value.  Here is a toy example:

(S <- matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 0, 0, 0, 5), 3, 3,
             dimnames = list(c("x1","x2","e"), c("x1","x2","e"))))
set.seed(123)
(dat <- as.data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(n = 50, mu = c(0, 0, 0), Sigma = S)))
dat$y <- 10 + 3*dat$x1 + 4*dat$x2 + dat$e
head(dat)
sapply(dat, var) # use these values in the model syntax below
model0 <- ' ## regression model
  y ~ b1*x1 + b2*x2
  ## define standardized estimates
  ## denominator = total observed variance of y
  ## numerators = observed variances of x1 & x2
  b1s := b1 * sqrt(1.519002 / 75.506641)
  b2s := b2 * sqrt(2.799830 / 75.506641)
'
## notice the newly defined parameters match the standardized output
fit0 <- sem(model0, data = dat)
summary(fit0, standardized = TRUE)
## now test this constraint
model1 <- c(model0, ' b1s == b2s ')
fit1 <- sem(model1, data = dat)
summary(fit1, standardized = TRUE) # raw slopes differ, std. slopes are ==
anova(fit0, fit1) # reject the null

If either is a latent variable, then the estimated variance of the latent predictor is a model parameter that is easily labeled and used in the equation for the defined (standardized) parameters.  If the outcome is latent, then you will need to define the total variance of the outcome as a sum of the estimated (and labeled) residual variance plus the model-implied explained variance (tracing rules or matrix algebra will help you here) -- then you use that defined parameter in the equation for the defined (standardized) parameters.

Terry
